walkthroughs.body_html:
Genetics, Populations & Ecosystems — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Genetics, Populations & Ecosystems brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Genetics, Populations & Ecosystems.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Small populations

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.

mcqs.q: What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.
They are random changes in DNA — caused by errors in replication or by mutagens — not directed by need.
Mutations occur because organisms need to adapt to their environment.
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Mutations only happen in organisms that have been damaged by external chemicals.
